extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of scientific criticism, reviewers of astronomical/physical claims, and authors of pamphlets/controversial theories (19th-century scientific and literary readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles for assessing and producing scientific claims, astronomical discoveries, and controversial pamphlets — covering verification, data sufficiency, literature familiarity, methodology, and tone in criticism. Emphasizes independent corroboration, systematic observation, and careful reading of sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent verification of calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: “The remarkable calculations of M. Le Verrier--which have pointed out, as now appears, nearly the true situation of the new planet, by resolving the inverse problem of the perturbations--if uncorroborated by repetition of the numerical calculations by another hand, or by independent investigation from another quarter, would hardly justify so strong an assurance as that conveyed by my expressions above alluded to.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong theoretical claims (e.g., predicting a planet's position) require independent repetition of numerical calculations or independent investigations before one can make emphatic assurances. Do not assert high confidence based on a single uncorroborated computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of observational data
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Adams 'did not consider [his approximation] to be worthy of confidence, on account of his not having employed a sufficient number of observations of Uranus.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid drawing firm conclusions from analyses that use too few observations. Ensure the dataset is large and varied enough to support the claimed results or orbital elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroboration by independent agreement increases confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: “The coincidence as to position from two entirely independent investigations naturally inspired confidence.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent investigations reaching similar results (e.g., predicted positions) bolster credibility. Seek or cite independent lines of evidence when asserting novel discoveries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish detailed methods to enable scrutiny and reproduction
rubrics_metrics.description: References to Mr. Adams's investigations being ‘published in detail’ and the need for corroboration imply publication of details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claiming theoretical or computational results, publish the full methods, intermediate computations, and data so others can reproduce and verify the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic, theory-guided observational search
rubrics_metrics.description: “The observations were directed, in the first instance, to the part of the heavens which theory had pointed out as the most probable place of the planet; in selecting which I was guided by a paper drawn up for me by Mr. Adams.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use theoretical predictions to prioritize and guide systematic searches. A targeted, theory-informed observing plan is more efficient than unguided searching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep and compare repeated positional records
rubrics_metrics.description: Challis recorded positions on July 30, Aug. 4, Aug. 12 and notes that comparison of observations at intervals would have shown the planet: 'A comparison of the observations of July 30 and August 12 would, according to the principle of search which I employed, have shown me the planet.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record multiple observations (with times/positions) and compare them across epochs to reveal moving objects; careful record-keeping and epoch-to-epoch comparison are essential in discovery claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow continued observations before approximating all orbital elements
rubrics_metrics.description: “The other elements of the orbit cannot be approximated to till the observations shall have been continued for a longer period.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize limits of short-term datasets: some parameters (e.g., orbital elements) require longer observational baselines to estimate reliably. Avoid overinterpreting limited early data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know and read the existing literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of the tide-theory author: 'he had read nothing on the subject' and the reviewer observes that had he read actual investigations he would have known terminology like the sun and moon being called 'planets' in tidal discussions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before proposing or criticizing theories, survey the relevant published work and terminology so as not to err through ignorance. Familiarity with prior investigations prevents elementary mistakes and misstatements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and use technical terminology correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: the reviewer rebukes the tide-theory author for objecting 'the Sun is no planet'—a misunderstanding of established usage in tidal theory; elsewhere Mr. Frost is suspected of misunderstanding 'centrifugal force.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure correct comprehension of domain-specific terms (even archaic or discipline-specific usages). Misunderstanding terminology leads to invalid objections and undermines credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not misread or take remarks out of intended context
rubrics_metrics.description: “A large class of the paradoxers, when they meet with something which taken in their sense is absurd, do not take the trouble to find out the intended meaning, but walk off with the words laden with their own first construction.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When encountering a puzzling or oddly phrased claim, investigate the intended meaning, context, and background before reacting. Avoid literal or surface-first readings that twist meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult primary sources rather than summaries or advertisements
rubrics_metrics.description: “A paradoxer should not stop at reading the advertisements of Newton or Laplace; he should learn to look at the stock of goods.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base critiques and learning on the original works (primary sources) rather than on summaries, reviews, or promotional material, which may omit crucial details or nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of confirmation bias and projecting one's own beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Regarding pamphleteers who allege conspiracies: 'The success of such writers in believing what they have a bias to believe, would, if they knew themselves, make them think it equally likely that the inculpated classes might really believe what it is their interest to believe.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of one's own biases when evaluating evidence. Do not assume other parties act from conspiratorial motives without evidence; consider simpler explanations and the likelihood of self-deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain fairness and avoid insulting tone in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: About a critical reviewer: 'He is not always just and never fails to insult.' Elsewhere the author praises 'moderate and respectful treatment' of controversial questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should be fair, proportionate, and respectful. Insulting or unfair rhetoric weakens arguments and undermines constructive discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be precise in phrasing and avoid assumption-tricks
rubrics_metrics.description: The author faults the 'assumption-trick' of controversy where one party assumes the opponent has not considered a topic (and notes Mr. Holyoake's phrasing led to such a presumption).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate challenges without implicitly misrepresenting the opponent's prior knowledge or intentions. Phrase requests and critiques precisely to avoid misleading implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check typographical/formatting context before leaping to conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: A misread shop window inscription 'Princess Alexandra! collar and cuff!' led to a false inference; also a book-back reading 'Blast the Antinomians!' was misinterpreted because of lack of a dividing line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider punctuation, layout, and surrounding visual/contextual cues that can change interpretation. Avoid hasty public reactions based on ambiguous presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historical and secondary sources to place claims in context
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to Professor Grant's 'History of Physical Astronomy' as an 'excellent account' of the Le Verrier/Adams matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing priority disputes or historical claims, consult authoritative histories and secondary literature to understand the broader context and earlier discussions.
